questions.scenario: A team needs at least 50 IPv4 addresses in one subnet, including infrastructure reservations. Which prefix is the smallest candidate with at least 64 total addresses?
questions.explanation: A /26 leaves 6 host bits and therefore 64 total addresses. Provider reservations can reduce usable capacity, so planning must distinguish total from usable addresses. [RFC 4632](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4632.html).

questions.scenario: A host is 10.20.4.10/24 and must send to 10.20.4.80. Its default gateway is healthy. What should it normally do first?

options.text: Send the packet to its default gateway
Resolve the destination as an on-link neighbor
Translate the source through NAT
Query DNS for the destination MAC

questions.explanation: Both addresses are in 10.20.4.0/24, so the destination is on-link. Neighbor discovery supplies the link-layer address; DNS and NAT solve different problems. [RFC 1122](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1122.html).

questions.scenario: Routes for 10.0.0.0/8, 10.40.0.0/16, and 0.0.0.0/0 all exist. Their metrics differ. Which route handles 10.40.8.9?

options.text: Whichever route was added first

questions.explanation: Routing chooses the most specific matching prefix, so /16 wins over /8 and /0. [RFC 1812](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1812.html).

questions.scenario: A platform team is choosing IPv4 space for internal-only application subnets. Which two ranges are private-use space defined by RFC 1918?
questions.explanation: 10.0.0.0/8 and 172.16.0.0/12 are private-use ranges. 198.51.100.0/24 is documentation space and 224.0.0.0/4 is multicast. [RFC 1918](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1918.html).

questions.scenario: A private worker reaches a public API through source NAT. Which statement best describes the change?

options.text: The worker's route table becomes public
A translator rewrites address information at a boundary
DNS replaces the private address permanently
The subnet prefix is extended across the internet

questions.explanation: NAT rewrites address and often port information at a translation boundary. It does not make private routes globally routable or turn DNS into a routing mechanism. [RFC 3022](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3022.html).

questions.scenario: Two networks that must be peered both use 10.30.0.0/16. Each already has active workloads. What is the core routing problem?

options.text: The duplicate prefix makes remote route selection ambiguous
Private addresses cannot cross any router
The /16 prefix has too few addresses for peering
Peering requires public DNS records

questions.explanation: Overlapping address space makes the same destination prefix mean different networks. Renumbering or an explicit translation design is needed. [RFC 1918](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1918.html).

questions.scenario: A /28 application subnet is nearly exhausted and autoscaling needs twenty more interfaces. What should be reviewed first?

options.text: The DNS TTL of the application hostname
TCP keepalive on existing instances
The default gateway MAC address
Address capacity and a non-overlapping larger or additional subnet plan

questions.explanation: The constraint is address capacity. Plan a larger or additional non-overlapping allocation while accounting for platform reservations and growth. [RFC 4632](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4632.html).

questions.scenario: A server capture sees client SYN packets, but the server has no route back to the client subnet. Which symptom is most likely?

options.text: The client times out because replies cannot be routed back
TLS reports an expired certificate
DNS returns NXDOMAIN
The listener changes to UDP

questions.explanation: Inbound arrival proves only the forward path. Without a return route, response packets cannot reach the client and the connection commonly times out. [RFC 1122](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1122.html).

questions.scenario: A dual-stack host has fe80::10/64 and 2001:db8:20::10/64. Both appear on one interface. Which two interpretations are correct?

options.text: fe80::10 is link-local and needs an interface context when ambiguity exists
Both addresses are IPv4 private space
2001:db8:20::10 has global unicast scope in this documentation scenario
Having IPv6 automatically bypasses firewall policy

questions.explanation: FE80::/10 is link-local. 2001:db8::/32 is reserved for documentation but demonstrates global-unicast addressing structure. IPv6 still requires deliberate filtering. [RFC 4291](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4291.html), [RFC 3849](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3849.html).

questions.scenario: A hostname has A and AAAA records, but only IPv4 succeeds. The TLS name is identical on both paths. What is the best next check?

options.text: Inspect IPv6 address, route, neighbor, and policy evidence separately from IPv4
Delete the A record immediately
Assume the certificate cannot support IPv6
Increase the IPv4 subnet size

questions.explanation: The two address families have separate addressing, routing, neighbor discovery, and filtering paths. Diagnose the failing IPv6 path rather than assuming DNS presence proves connectivity. [RFC 8200](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8200.html).
